entry.title: Pharmaceutical Leaders Express Skepticism Over Silicon Valley Claims That AI Will Cure Diseases
entry.content:
Links: wsj.com

Pharmaceutical executives are pushing back against claims from technology figures that artificial intelligence will cure most diseases within the coming decade. Industry leaders argue that biological complexity presents fundamental obstacles that algorithms alone cannot easily overcome, noting that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has yet to grant clearance to any AI-designed drug.

While numerous AI-driven drug candidates have advanced into clinical trials, critics emphasize that unstandardized training data and a lack of proven clinical validation separate algorithmic promise from medical reality. Executives contend that technology companies often underestimate the intricacies of human biology and the rigorous regulatory standards required for pharmaceutical approval.

entry.title: California Public Utilities Commission Rejects Trump Administration Demand to Scrap State Net Neutrality Laws
entry.content:
Links: arstechnica.com | cpuc.ca.gov

California has signed a final agreement to accept $1.42 billion in federal broadband grant funding through the Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment program while explicitly rejecting a Trump administration condition requiring states to exempt internet service providers from net neutrality and rate regulations. In a letter to the National Telecommunications and Information Administration, the California Public Utilities Commission stated it will not be bound by unconstitutional terms and has reserved the right to challenge the federal mandate in court before distributing any funds to providers.

The dispute centers on Section 50 of the program's rules, which prohibits recipient states from enforcing utility-style regulations on broadband providers for up to 14 years. State officials and consumer advocacy groups argue the federal agency lacks the statutory authority to preempt state laws like California's net neutrality and emergency throttling protections, though legal experts note that funding distribution will remain on hold until federal and state officials resolve the disagreement or a court intervenes.

entry.title: Hundreds of AI Apps on Apple and Google App Stores Hid Sexually Abusive Deepfake Features
entry.content:

An investigation by WIRED and security researchers has uncovered a network of more than 400 applications and domains disguised as mundane tools, such as pet portrait generators and workout apps, that secretly feature sexually abusive deepfake tools. These applications bypassed review processes on Apple’s App Store and Google’s Play Store by dynamically loading hidden web interfaces that generate explicit images and videos from uploaded user photos.

The network, linked to Chinese developers and a Hong Kong entity named KeLing Technology Limited, was heavily promoted through tens of thousands of deceptive video ads on Meta platforms like Facebook and Instagram. Although tech companies have since removed many of the associated apps and banned related ad accounts, the operation highlights ongoing vulnerabilities in app store vetting and ad moderation systems that allow harmful deepfake features to evade detection.

entry.title: Federal Judge Allows NAACP Clean Air Act Lawsuit Against xAI to Proceed
entry.content:
Links: techcrunch.com | earthjustice.org

A federal judge has denied a motion by xAI to dismiss a Clean Air Act lawsuit brought by the NAACP and the Southern Environmental Law Center. The litigation accuses the AI company of operating dozens of gas combustion turbines without required preconstruction or operating permits to power its Colossus data center near Memphis.

xAI had argued that the lawsuit should be thrown out because the turbines qualify as mobile sources and are thus exempt from permits, while also challenging the plaintiffs' standing. Judge Debra M. Brown rejected these arguments, affirming that the plaintiffs have statutory standing and that citizen suits do not violate the Constitution. The case moves forward amid growing public scrutiny and regulatory pushback against the environmental impact of large data centers.
